title: Sell Mineral Rights in Wyoming County, PA
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Wyoming County, PA | Dry Gas Marcellus
metaDescription: Own minerals in Wyoming County, PA? We buy dry-gas Marcellus interests directly across Tunkhannock and the county, with a real title review first.
heroLead: Wyoming County anchors Pennsylvania's northeastern dry gas corridor, developed heavily by Cabot Oil & Gas and now managed largely by Coterra Energy.
intro: We didn't grow up in Wyoming County, our family's own story runs through a different part of the state, but we've spent enough time here over the years to understand what makes it different from the wet gas counties further southwest. This is dry gas country, methane-heavy production without the liquids premium, developed by a smaller handful of operators who moved in early and stayed.

That concentration of activity is actually useful for mineral owners here. It means there's real production history behind most Wyoming County interests, and we use that history to give you an honest, specific number rather than a generic county-wide guess.

sections.heading: Cabot's Deep Footprint, Now Coterra's
paragraphs: Cabot Oil & Gas was the dominant operator developing Wyoming County's Marcellus acreage from the earliest years of the play, running some of the most heavily developed dry gas units in the entire northeastern corridor. Following its 2021 merger with Cimarex Energy, that acreage and production is now largely managed under the Coterra Energy name.

If your family's lease or royalty statements still reference Cabot, that's normal, the underlying operations transferred to Coterra, but the lease terms you originally signed generally remain the governing document unless formally amended.

sections.heading: The County Seat and Where Records Live
paragraphs: Tunkhannock, the county seat, houses the Wyoming County recorder of deeds, where we confirm the chain of title on every interest we evaluate. Because so much of this county's leasing happened in a relatively concentrated period during the boom years, deed and lease records here tend to be somewhat more consistent in format than in counties with longer, more scattered drilling histories.

That consistency helps, but it doesn't eliminate the real work of tracing an interest through multiple generations of a family, especially where probate wasn't completed cleanly or a deed reference points to a boundary description that's since changed.

sections.heading: Dry Gas Value and Why It's Often Underestimated
paragraphs: Because Wyoming County's gas is dry, without the ethane and propane that boost wet gas pricing, owners here sometimes assume their interest is worth less than a comparable interest in the wet gas counties down south. That's not always true. Many Wyoming County units have posted exceptionally strong volumes over a long production life, and steady high-volume dry gas production can still add up to significant cumulative value.
We evaluate based on your unit's actual volume and revenue history rather than assuming dry gas automatically means a lower number.

sections.heading: The Deduction Language Behind Coterra and Legacy Cabot Leases
paragraphs: Pennsylvania's Guaranteed Minimum Royalty Act sets the floor at one-eighth net, and post-production cost deductions, gathering, compression, dehydration, marketing, are generally permitted above that floor under the Kilmer v. Elexco framework. Some of the earliest Cabot-era leases in this county carried broad deduction language that has drawn scrutiny in litigation over the years statewide.

We read your lease's actual deduction clause closely, because the difference between a narrowly written clause and a broadly written one can meaningfully change what your net royalty should look like.

sections.heading: Act 13 Impact Fees Fund the County, Not You Directly
paragraphs: Wyoming County collects Act 13 impact fee revenue from unconventional wells drilled here, funding that supports road repair, emergency services, and local infrastructure. That revenue is separate from your personal royalty and does not get distributed to individual mineral owners, a distinction we make sure every owner we talk to understands clearly.

faqs.question: Why does my royalty statement now say Coterra instead of Cabot?
faqs.answer: Cabot Oil & Gas merged with Cimarex Energy in 2021 to form Coterra Energy. Your original lease terms typically remain in effect unless formally amended, even though the operating company name changed.

faqs.question: Is dry gas from Wyoming County worth less than wet gas from southwestern Pennsylvania?
faqs.answer: Dry gas sells for less per unit than liquids-rich wet gas, but strong, sustained volumes in this county can still add up to significant value. We evaluate your specific unit's production rather than assuming based on gas type alone.

faqs.question: What is the Kilmer v. Elexco decision and how does it affect me?
faqs.answer: It's a Pennsylvania court ruling that upheld an operator's right to deduct reasonable post-production costs from royalties, as long as the payment stays above the one-eighth net floor. It's shaped how most Marcellus-era leases, including many in Wyoming County, are enforced today.

faqs.question: Does the Act 13 impact fee pay mineral owners?
faqs.answer: No. It funds county and municipal infrastructure and services, separate from the royalty paid under your individual lease.

faqs.question: How do you handle interests where probate was never fully completed?
faqs.answer: We can often advise on what's needed to clear up an incomplete probate, and in some cases work with the interest through alternative documentation. Every situation is different, so tell us where things stand.

faqs.question: Do you buy interests anywhere in Wyoming County, or only near Tunkhannock?
faqs.answer: We evaluate interests throughout the county, well beyond the area near the county seat. Location within the county affects which unit and operator applies, but not whether we'll take a look.
